 Voltage glitching unlocks up to 80GB of VRAM on Nvidia CMP-170HX mining cards
 Thursday, 12 November 2026, 12:40 
 Photo source: Tom's Hardware 
 Kate’s voltage-modification technique enabled up to 80GB of VRAM on her test cards; one card delivered 20% more FP16 FMA performance than a standard A100. 
 Used data center GPUs are one option for enthusiasts building local AI clusters. A software mod called CMPunlocker already unlocks features on Nvidia CMP-170HX cards. Kate’s hardware modification goes further by using voltage glitches to change the cards’ fuse-controller settings.
 This is reported by Tom's Hardware .
 Kate based her approach on a paper describing an exploit for GA100 cards’ microcode. She targeted the onboard fuse controller, which is normally used at the factory to disable chip components that did not pass testing, allowing them to be sold in lower-end configurations.
 Advertisement 
 The GA100 silicon contains the corresponding HBM2e memory dies, even when some are disabled at the factory, much like shader modules. The 8GB CMP-170HX variant is based on a GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e, while 10GB cards use a 40GB GA100.
 The cards have 16,384 eFuses arranged in a 512 x 32 array. Reading them reveals a card’s configuration, including its VRAM sections, shader modules, PCIe 4.0, NVLink and video-codec hardware. Kate said Nvidia’s design is insecure because changing fuses can enable more features rather than restrict them.
 Users normally cannot write to the fuses. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to connect to power signals on the card’s PCB. The board intercepted PWM signals sent to the voltage-regulator controller and induced voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller is located.
 Kate repeatedly read fuse statuses in a tight loop while applying the glitches. This put the controller in a state where its security-bit settings allowed writes. She made sure to disable any shader modules already marked as defective before reconfiguring the cards, since the physical fuses cannot be reset.
 After testing multiple workloads, Kate found that nine of her cards had all 80GB of VRAM working, while one had 64GB usable. Unlocking all shader modules gave her 20% more FP16 FMA performance than a regular A100. She attributed this to the chips often having 120 or more usable shader modules, compared with the 108 listed in the specifications. A GA100 die starts with 128 shader modules to account for manufacturing defects.
 CMPunlocker is needed to enable the newly available features in the drivers, but the software mod alone leaves limits in place: a 40-64GB VRAM ceiling depending on the card variant, locked shader modules and PCIe bandwidth limited to 2.0. It also does not provide ECC, NVLink or multi-instance GPU support, features used in server setups and for product segmentation.
 Kate’s voltage mod removes those limits. Her best test card ran at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She did not test the video-encoder hardware.
 Advertisement 
 A CMP-170HX with 8GB of memory currently costs around $3,000, while the 10GB version costs around $2,500. An Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can cost $20,000 or more. SXM server-module versions are cheaper but require supporting infrastructure. The prices may vary significantly as more people learn about the modifications.
 Kate said she is publishing her research because another person independently found the same issue. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though the company has limited options for cards already on the market.
